title_en: AI writing assistants and graded schoolwork
title_he: עוזרי כתיבה מבוססי בינה מלאכותית ועבודות להגשה
prompt: Argue whether secondary schools should allow students to use AI writing assistants when they produce graded written assignments, and respond to opposing views.

instructions.en: Write an analytical argumentative essay of 800-1000 words for an educated general reader, for example the readers of an education magazine. Define your key terms precisely: "using an AI assistant" can mean brainstorming, getting feedback, drafting, rewriting or correcting, and your thesis should say which uses you mean and for which tasks. Your position may be conditional, but it must be clear. Plan before you write: an introduction with context, definitions and thesis; body paragraphs that each develop one point with analysis and support and link back to the thesis; one serious objection discussed in depth (not several listed briefly) and placed before the conclusion; and a conclusion that synthesises without adding new arguments. Consider at least two perspectives, such as learners, teachers and fairness in assessment. Distinguish what is known from what is likely and what is speculation, and calibrate your language accordingly. Draw on your own experience as a learner and on reasoned examples; do not invent studies or statistics. Before you revise, score your draft against the rubric yourself.

required_elements: an introduction that defines key terms and states a precise thesis
at least three body arguments, each developing one point with analysis and support
consideration of the issue from at least two perspectives (e.g. learners, teachers, fairness in assessment)
one serious objection discussed in depth, fairly stated, attributed and placed before the conclusion
a rebuttal based on reasoning or evidence, with the thesis refined if you concede a point
a conclusion that synthesises the argument and adds no new arguments

checklist.en: Claim: my thesis is precise and debatable: it says which kinds of AI use I mean, at which stages of writing, and for which tasks.

Reasons: each body paragraph develops one reason, opens with a clear topic sentence and links back to the thesis; the paragraphs build the argument in order, and together they consider at least two perspectives (for example learners and teachers).
Evidence: each reason is supported by analysis and specific, relevant examples; I distinguish what is known from what is likely, and I have not invented studies or figures.
Counterargument: I discuss one serious objection in depth, state it as its supporters would, and place it before the conclusion.
Rebuttal: I answer the objection with reasoning or evidence, and if I concede part of it, my thesis is refined accordingly.
Conclusion: my conclusion synthesises the argument and its implications without introducing new arguments.

scaffold.en: Define the terms: list the different ways a student might use an AI assistant, and decide which of them your thesis covers.
Write a working thesis and test it against a hard case, such as a student with dyslexia or a take-home exam.
Essay blueprint: introduction (context, definitions, thesis), three body paragraphs (one point each), objection and rebuttal, conclusion. Write one sentence for each section before drafting.
Choose the single strongest objection. Decide your rebuttal move and whether it forces you to refine the thesis.
After drafting, reverse-outline: write the main point of each paragraph in one line. Does each point support the thesis, and does the order build?

exemplar.outline:
Parallel prompt (not your question; read this only after you have written your own essay): Argue whether cities should allow shared electric scooters (rented through an app and left on the street after use), and respond to opposing views.

Thesis: Cities should allow shared electric scooters only under clear conditions (a speed limit, no riding on pavements and parking in marked zones), because the scooters can replace some short car journeys and make public transport easier to reach, yet without rules they shift risk and clutter onto pedestrians.

I. Introduction: context (shared scooters arrived in many cities before any rules existed); definitions (shared vs. privately owned scooters; riding on roads and cycle lanes vs. riding on pavements); thesis.
II. Body 1, short journeys: some car journeys in a city are only a few kilometres long; analysis: a scooter replaces them only if it is as quick and convenient as the car, which depends on parking zones near homes and destinations.
III. Body 2, access to public transport: a long walk to the nearest station puts people off using it; a scooter can shorten that walk, especially in areas with few bus routes.
IV. Body 3, pedestrians (annotated below): fast, almost silent vehicles on pavements, and scooters left lying across the path, shift risk onto people who never ride them.
V. Objection: "Speed and parking rules cannot be enforced, so scooters should simply be banned." Rebuttal: concede that occasional police checks do not work; refine the thesis so that the rules are built into the service (lower speeds set automatically in busy streets, rides that cannot end outside a parking zone) and operators lose their licence if they do not comply.
VI. Conclusion: the question is not whether but on what terms; restate the conditional thesis; implication for how cities license new transport services.
exemplar.annotated_paragraph:
From the exemplar essay on the parallel prompt above (section IV: third body paragraph)

[1] The strongest reason for strict conditions, however, concerns the people who never ride a scooter at all. [2] A pavement works because everyone on it moves at roughly walking pace, so pedestrians can predict one another's movements without thinking about it. [3] A scooter travelling several times faster, almost silently, breaks this unspoken agreement: an older person stepping out of a doorway or a blind pedestrian following the edge of a wall may not hear it in time, and a scooter left lying across the path becomes an obstacle for anyone using a wheelchair or pushing a pram. [4] This matters beyond individual collisions, because people who no longer feel safe on the pavement may simply go out less, and those most affected are often the people with the fewest alternatives. [5] It is this shift of risk onto pedestrians, rather than any dislike of new technology, that justifies keeping scooters off pavements and requiring them to be parked in marked zones.

Notes
[1] Topic sentence: one point only, signalled as the strongest, with a transition ("however") that contrasts it with the previous paragraph.
[2] Analysis begins by explaining the mechanism (a shared walking pace), so the claim does not rest on assertion.
[3] Concrete illustrations of the mechanism, drawn from more than one group of pedestrians. "May not hear it in time" describes a risk without inventing accident figures.
[4] Extends the consequence to a second perspective (people who may stop going out), which adds depth rather than repetition; "may" and "often" calibrate claims the writer cannot prove with data.
[5] The concluding sentence links back to the thesis and limits its scope precisely ("off pavements", "marked zones").
